Abraham Calov
a'bra-ham kah'lov
n. (Abraham Calov, 1612–1686, Wittenberg theologian, systematician and opponent of syncretism)
Hebrew Abraham, father of a multitude; Calov, latinised from the German surname Kalau.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Abraham Calov taught at Wittenberg for forty years and produced a systematic theology in twelve volumes, a vast annotated Bible written largely against the readings of Hugo Grotius, and a long shelf of polemic. His principal controversy was with Georg Calixtus of Helmstedt, who proposed that Lutherans, Reformed and Romanists might unite on the Apostles' Creed and the consensus of the first five centuries; Calov opposed that programme as a dissolution of the faith and gave it the name by which it is still known, syncretism. The dictionary judges the controversy in halves. Calov was right that a union built on the first five centuries would quietly surrender justification by faith alone, which is not in the Creed and is in Paul; he was wrong, and sometimes unlovely, in treating the Reformed as the Creed's enemies rather than as brethren who confessed the same gospel and differed on the Supper. His Bible, as it happens, was the copy Johann Sebastian Bach owned and annotated.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines syncretism as the attempted union of different systems, and systematic as formed with regular connection of parts.

expand to see more

SYN'CRETISM, n. The attempted union of principles or parties irreconcilably at variance with each other.

SYSTEMAT'IC, a. Methodical; formed with regular connection and adaptation of parts to each other.

CONSENT', n. Agreement of minds in opinion; accord.

POLEM'ICS, n. Controversy; the practice of disputation on points of doctrine.

Key Scripture

Gal 2:5 — "To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you."

Jud 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

Rom 3:28 — "Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law."

Eph 4:14 — "That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;"

Modern Corruption

He named and fought syncretism, rightly on justification and wrongly in treating the Reformed as enemies.

expand to see more

The error to name is syncretism as Calov defined it: a union of churches purchased by reducing the faith to what all parties can still say, which in practice means the ancient creeds without the article the Reformation recovered. The Apostles' Creed does not teach justification by faith alone; a communion built on the Creed alone can therefore include Trent. Calov saw that and was right. The corresponding modern form is any ecumenism that treats the gospel's instrumental cause as a secondary matter.

The standard is Paul's refusal at Jerusalem and his conclusion in Romans. “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5). “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28). The faith was delivered once and is to be contended for: “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). And the aim of all of it is a church that is not blown about — “carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14) — which is a different thing from a church at war with its brethren.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hupotage (G5292), subjection; Greek anemos (G417), a wind.

expand to see more

Greek hupotage (G5292) — subjection, submission; Galatians 2:5.

Greek diameno (G1265) — to continue, to remain throughout; Galatians 2:5.

Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, to justify; Romans 3:28.

Greek anemos (G417) — a wind; Ephesians 4:14.

Greek kludonizomai (G2831) — to be tossed as by waves; Ephesians 4:14.

Usage

"“no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5) — against the Helmstedt programme."

"“a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28) — the article the Creed does not contain."

"“carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14) — twelve volumes, and Bach's own Bible."
